think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 71-year-old woman with a decade-long history of poorly controlled tophaceous gout and rheumatoid arthritis presents with left lower back pain, difficulty walking, and a large cystic multilocular iliopsoas/hip lesion. Given marked hyperuricemia (555.9 umol/L), periarticular sandy calcifications, and milky aspirate, the presentation strongly suggests an extensive gouty tophus. However, the subsequent emergence of persistent cyclical nocturnal high-grade spikes (up to 39.3°C) unresponsive to broad-spectrum cephalosporins and urate-lowering agents signals an occult granulomatous coinfection within the retroperitoneal tophus.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission breakpoint falls on Day 1 after initial clinical examination, triage blood work, urinalysis, plain pelvic radiographs, and abdominal/pelvic CT, before the onset of cyclical high-grade fevers on Day 2, needle aspiration of milky fluid on Day 3, T-cell interferon testing, and high-throughput metagenomic tissue sequencing.
3. Differential Distinctions: Uncomplicated tophaceous gout of the iliopsoas (does not cause persistent spiking fevers up to 39.3°C or severe acute-phase reactant elevations refractory to NSAIDs/febuxostat), pyogenic psoas abscess (ruled out by negative standard bacterial/anaerobic cultures and failure of 8 days of IV ceftriaxone), and fungal abscess (ruled out by negative fungal smears and cultures). T-cell IGRA positivity and tissue mNGS proving Mycobacterium tuberculosis establish coinfection.
case_prompt:
A 71-year-old woman who lived alone was admitted to the hospital with left lower back pain, fatigue, and difficulty walking. She had previously been hospitalized at another institution for approximately one month and treated with bed rest, analgesics, and empiric systemic anti-infectives without symptomatic improvement. Her medical history was notable for poorly controlled gout and rheumatoid arthritis for more than 10 years; she denied a history of diabetes mellitus, prior pulmonary disease, genetic disorders, or trauma. Physical examination revealed deforming changes of the right hands and palpable tophi in the left finger joints of over a decade's duration. There was moderate tenderness in the left lower quadrant of the abdomen, restricted range of motion of the left hip, and posterolateral swelling of the left hip with an obvious concave scar, without sinus tracts or open wounds. She was afebrile on admission.

Initial laboratory investigations revealed a serum uric acid level of 555.9 µmol/L (reference range: 208–428 µmol/L), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 113 mm/h (reference range: 1–15 mm/h), C-reactive protein (CRP) of 182.59 mg/L (reference range: 0–5 mg/L), procalcitonin of 0.67 ng/mL, white blood cell count of 8.04 x 10⁹/L (78.8% neutrophils, 12.9% lymphocytes), hemoglobin of 54 g/L, and platelet count of 221 x 10⁹/L. Serum creatinine was elevated at 191 µmol/L and blood urea nitrogen at 11.9 mmol/L; serum albumin was 26.3 g/L. Urinalysis was unremarkable except for positive occult blood (+). Stool examination, electrocardiogram, echocardiography, and plain chest radiography were all normal.

Pelvic radiographs demonstrated erosion of the left sacral and iliac borders, widening of the left sacroiliac joint, condensation of the adjacent bone, joint space narrowing, and a low-density cystic lesion of the left hip. Computed tomography (CT) confirmed widening of the left sacroiliac joint, a multilocular fluid collection within the left psoas muscle, and juxta-articular soft-tissue masses containing sandy calcifications around the pelvis and bilateral hips.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Isolated retroperitoneal and hip tophaceous gout
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: While the patient had marked hyperuricemia, deforming peripheral tophi, and sandy calcifications on CT, isolated tophaceous gout could not explain the persistent cyclical nocturnal fever (peaking at 39.3°C) that began on day 2 and failed to respond to febuxostat and NSAIDs.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: CT findings indicated the possibility of a combined left psoas muscle and left hip abscess, as well as tophaceous gout of both hips... On the 2nd day of admission, febuxostat 40 mg was administered orally once a day for the gout treatment; ceftriaxone 2 g intravenous drip was used once a day for anti-infective therapy lasting 8 days, but it did not work as the fever persisted.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Pyogenic bacterial or fungal psoas abscess
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Pyogenic bacterial abscess and fungal collections were ruled out because 8 days of IV ceftriaxone failed to alleviate symptoms, and multiple aspirated fluid and surgical tissue cultures were negative for Gram-positive, Gram-negative, anaerobic bacteria, and fungi.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: cultures for Gram-positive and Gram-negative bacteria, anaerobic bacteria, and fungi were all negative. Quantitative fluorescence polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of DNA in tuberculosis sputum smears for acid-fast bacteria and fungi was also negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: T-cell interferon detection returned positive, and subsequent open debridement of the iliopsoas collection combined with high-throughput metagenomic gene sequencing confirmed divergent Mycobacterium tuberculosis co-infecting the gouty tophus.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: however, the detection of TB infection in the T cells was positive... high-throughput gene sequencing of these tissues for various pathogens indicated divergent Mycobacterium tuberculosis without other bacteria, fungi, or anaerobic bacteria.

editor_comments: Distilled case accurately targets Tuberculosis (iliopsoas gout-TB coinfection). Breakpoint placed at Day 1 triage before aspiration and send-out sequencing. Zero pathogen names in case prompt.
